title: High / Low Pricing Strategies
content:
Pricing a home correctly from day one is critical. The initial price sets the market’s perception of value, and buyers subconsciously categorize homes based on this first impression. A well-strategized price ensures maximum interest while avoiding the stigma of a property that lingers on the market.

High vs. Low Pricing Approaches: Which Works Best?

Starting High and Adjusting DownThis approach can work in strong seller markets with low inventory, where buyers may be willing to negotiate. However, if overpriced, a home can quickly become ‘stale,’ leading to price cuts and diminished buyer interest.
Starting Just Below Market to Drive DemandPricing slightly below market value—relative to similar homes in the area—can generate multiple offers, creating a competitive bidding situation that drives the price up. This is effective in high-demand areas or when aiming for a fast sale.

Important note: When referring to “low” pricing in this context, it does not mean undervaluing a home. Instead, it refers to pricing just below the market for a particular home’s area and traits to strategically attract buyers and create competition.

Pricing to Sell vs. Pricing to Negotiate

  • Pricing to Sell means setting a realistic, market-driven price that generates immediate, serious interest.
  • Pricing to Negotiate often involves padding the price to allow room for offers, but this can backfire if buyers perceive the home as overpriced and do not engage at all.

Fear of Missing Out (FOMO) Pricing: Creating Buyer Urgency

  • A well-priced home generates strong interest, leading buyers to feel that if they don’t act quickly, they may lose the opportunity.
  • Homes that receive offers in the first week often sell at or above asking price, reinforcing the importance of proper pricing.
  • Conversely, a home that lingers on the market can give buyers the impression that ‘something must be wrong’ with the property, even if it’s just mispriced.
